
```lean
False.elim.{u} {C : Sort u} (h : False) : C
```
***
`False.elim : False → C` says that from `False`, any desired proposition
`C` holds. Also known as ex falso quodlibet (EFQ) or the principle of explosion.

The target type is actually `C : Sort u` which means it works for both
propositions and types. When executed, this acts like an "unreachable"
instruction: it is **undefined behavior** to run, but it will probably print
"unreachable code". (You would need to construct a proof of false to run it
anyway, which you can only do using `sorry` or unsound axioms.)

***
*import Init.Prelude*

```lean
rfl.{u} {α : Sort u} {a : α} : a = a
```
***
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.

and `(hn h).elim` will prove anything.

```lean
rfl.{u} {α : Sort u} {a : α} : a = a
```
***
`rfl : a = a` is the unique constructor of the equality type. This is the
same as `Eq.refl` except that it takes `a` implicitly instead of explicitly.

This is a more powerful theorem than it may appear at first, because although
the statement of the theorem is `a = a`, Lean will allow anything that is
definitionally equal to that type. So, for instance, `2 + 2 = 4` is proven in
Lean by `rfl`, because both sides are the same up to definitional equality.

type-dependent, but it is intended to be used for additive torsors. 
***
*import Mathlib.Algebra.Group.Defs*

```lean
EuclideanGeometry.orthogonalProjection.{u_1, u_2} {V : Type u_1} {P : Type u_2} [NormedAddCommGroup V]
  [InnerProductSpace ℝ V] [MetricSpace P] [NormedAddTorsor V P] (s : AffineSubspace ℝ P) [Nonempty ↥s]
  [HasOrthogonalProjection s.direction] : P →ᵃ[ℝ] ↥s
```
***
The orthogonal projection of a point onto a nonempty affine
subspace, whose direction is complete. The corresponding linear map
(mapping a vector to the difference between the projections of two
points whose difference is that vector) is the `orthogonalProjection`
for real inner product spaces, onto the direction of the affine
subspace being projected onto.

```lean
EuclideanGeometry.reflection_orthogonal_vadd.{u_1, u_2} {V : Type u_1} {P : Type u_2} [NormedAddCommGroup V]
  [InnerProductSpace ℝ V] [MetricSpace P] [NormedAddTorsor V P] {s : AffineSubspace ℝ P} [Nonempty ↥s]
  [HasOrthogonalProjection s.direction] {p : P} (hp : p ∈ s) {v : V} (hv : v ∈ s.directionᗮ) :
  (reflection s) (v +ᵥ p) = -v +ᵥ p
```
***
Reflecting an orthogonal vector plus a point in the subspace
produces the negation of that vector plus the point.

```lean
Submodule.smul_mem.{u, v} {R : Type u} {M : Type v} [Semiring R] [AddCommMonoid M] {module_M : Module R M}
  (p : Submodule R M) {x : M} (r : R) (h : x ∈ p) : r • x ∈ p
```
***
*import Mathlib.Algebra.Module.Submodule.Basic*

```lean
EuclideanGeometry.vsub_orthogonalProjection_mem_direction_orthogonal.{u_1, u_2} {V : Type u_1} {P : Type u_2}
  [NormedAddCommGroup V] [InnerProductSpace ℝ V] [MetricSpace P] [NormedAddTorsor V P] (s : AffineSubspace ℝ P)
  [Nonempty ↥s] [HasOrthogonalProjection s.direction] (p : P) : p -ᵥ ↑((orthogonalProjection s) p) ∈ s.directionᗮ
```
***
Subtracting the `orthogonalProjection` from `p` produces a result
in the orthogonal direction.

```lean
EuclideanGeometry.reflection_vadd_smul_vsub_orthogonalProjection.{u_1, u_2} {V : Type u_1} {P : Type u_2}
  [NormedAddCommGroup V] [InnerProductSpace ℝ V] [MetricSpace P] [NormedAddTorsor V P] {s : AffineSubspace ℝ P}
  [Nonempty ↥s] [HasOrthogonalProjection s.direction] {p₁ : P} (p₂ : P) (r : ℝ) (hp₁ : p₁ ∈ s) :
  (reflection s) (r • (p₂ -ᵥ ↑((orthogonalProjection s) p₂)) +ᵥ p₁) =
    -(r • (p₂ -ᵥ ↑((orthogonalProjection s) p₂))) +ᵥ p₁
```
***
Reflecting a vector plus a point in the subspace produces the
negation of that vector plus the point if the vector is a multiple of
the result of subtracting a point's orthogonal projection from that
point.
